entry:
Set of names by which an individual person or animal is known.

Also called a full name or prosoponym (from [[Ancient Greek]] *prósōpon*, "person," and *onoma*, "name"), it is in many cultures synonymous with the birth name or legal name.

In Western culture, nearly everyone has at least one given name (first name, forename, or Christian name) and a [[Surname|surname]] (last name or family name), which generally indicates membership in a family, tribe, or clan. In Arabic culture and in parts of Africa and Asia, a person's name is joined to a chain of names that begins with the father's name and usually ends with a family or tribe name. Some cultures add patronymics or matronymics, as in the middle name of [[Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky]] (whose father's given name was Ilya) or the last name of [[Björk]] Guðmundsdóttir. Some people are known by a single name and are called mononymous.

Surnames came into common use in China beginning in the 3rd century BC, in France in the 13th century, and in Germany in the 16th century; in Japan they did not become prevalent until the 19th century. Spain and most Latin American countries use two surnames. In Russia the middle name is a patronymic. Iceland still does not use surnames for its native inhabitants. The [[United Nations]] Convention on the Rights of the Child declares that a child has the right to a name from birth.

Behavioral, cognitive, and emotional patterns that make up an individual's unique, time-dependent adjustment to life.

Personality is relatively stable but can change over time through experience and developmental processes. There is no consensus on its definition; most theories focus on traits, [[Motivation|motivation]], skills, and [[Identity (social science)|identity]]. [[Personality psychology]] seeks to explain the characteristics that underlie differences in behavior, and personality is related to life outcomes such as work and relationship success, mental health, well-being, and longevity. Approaches to its study can be organized across dispositional, biological, intrapsychic (psychodynamic), cognitive-experiential, social and cultural, and adjustment domains. They reflect the influence of early theorists including [[Sigmund Freud]], Alfred Adler, [[Gordon Allport]], Hans Eysenck, [[Abraham Maslow]], and [[Carl Rogers]]. Psychodynamic theory stresses unconscious conflicts and early childhood experiences, humanistic theory emphasizes personal growth and self-actualization, and trait theory treats stable dispositional characteristics as the core of personality.

Personality is measured with objective tests and projective measures, among them the Big Five Inventory, the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI-2), and the Rorschach Inkblot test. The approach with the most support in the field is the Big Five: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (or emotional stability). These components are generally stable over time, and about half of the variance appears attributable to a person's genetics rather than environment. Personality changes much more quickly during childhood, so personality constructs in children are called temperament, regarded as the precursor to personality.

Naturally occurring yellowish-black liquid mixture consisting primarily of hydrocarbons, found in geological formations.

Also called crude oil or simply oil, the term covers both unprocessed crude and refined petroleum products. Petroleum is a [[Fossil fuel]] formed over millions of years from the anaerobic decay of buried prehistoric organisms, particularly plankton and algae. An estimated 70% of the world's deposits formed during the [[Mesozoic]]. Reserves are recovered mainly by drilling; unconventional reserves such as oil sands and oil shale are recovered by methods such as fracking. Oil is then refined, most easily by distillation, into products including [[Gasoline|gasoline]] (petrol), diesel, kerosene, jet fuel, [[Bitumen|bitumen]], lubricants, and thousands of other petrochemicals. The world consumes about 100 million barrels (16 million cubic metres) each day.

The word comes from Medieval Latin *petroleum* ("rock oil"), used in southern Italian monasteries by the end of the first millennium. Use of petroleum products is ancient: more than 4,300 years ago the [[Sumer|Sumerians]] used bitumen to make boats. By 347 CE oil was produced from bamboo-drilled wells in China, and in the 9th century oil fields were exploited around modern [[Baku]], Azerbaijan.

Petroleum production played a key role in industrialization after the Second Industrial Revolution, and some petroleum-rich countries, known as petrostates, gained significant economic and international influence in the latter half of the 20th century. Petroleum is non-renewable, and its extraction, refining, and burning release large quantities of greenhouse gases, making it a major contributor to anthropogenic [[Climate change|climate change]]. Production is estimated to reach peak oil before 2035, while the transition to renewable energy and increased electrification is expected to reduce dependency on petroleum.

Archipelagic country in Southeast Asia, in the western Pacific Ocean (pop. over 114 million).

Officially the Republic of the Philippines, it consists of about 7,641 islands with a total area of about 300,000 sq km, grouped into three main divisions: [[Luzon]], [[Visayas]], and [[Mindanao]]. It is the world's thirteenth-most-populous country. [[Manila]] is the capital and Quezon City the most populous city, both within Metro Manila.

Negritos, the archipelago's earliest known modern inhabitants, were followed by Austronesian peoples who arrived from Taiwan around 2200 BC. Animism, Hinduism with Buddhist influence, and Islam established island kingdoms. The arrival of [[Ferdinand Magellan]] began Spanish colonization; Catholicism became the dominant religion.

The [[Philippine Revolution]] began in 1896 and became entwined with the 1898 Spanish–American War. Spain ceded the territory to the United States,. The ensuing [[Philippine–American War]] ended with U.S. control, which lasted until the Japanese invasion during World War II. The Philippines became independent in 1946. Martial law under [[Ferdinand Marcos]] began in 1972, and his overthrow by the People Power Revolution in 1986 returned the country to democracy.

The economy is that of an emerging market and newly industrialized country, shifting from agriculture toward services and manufacturing. It continues to struggle with inequality, widespread corruption, and vulnerability to earthquakes, monsoon rains, and typhoons because it lies within the Pacific Ring of Fire. A 2016 international arbitral ruling rejected China's "nine-dash line" claims in the South China Sea and affirmed Philippine rights within its exclusive economic zone, though enforcement remains contested.

Systematic study of general and fundamental questions concerning existence, knowledge, mind, reason, language, and value.

The word comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] *philosophía*, "love of wisdom," from *phílos* ("loving, friend of") and *sophía* ("wisdom"). Some sources say the term was coined by the pre-Socratic philosopher [[Pythagoras]], but this is not certain. It entered English from Old French and Anglo-Norman around 1175 CE. Philosophy is a rational and critical inquiry that reflects on its own methods and assumptions. Socrates stated that "the unexamined life is not worth living" to highlight its role in understanding one's own existence.

Before the modern age the term was used in a wide sense that included most forms of rational inquiry, with [[Natural philosophy]] encompassing physics, chemistry, and biology. Isaac Newton's 1687 *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* referred to natural philosophy in its title but is today considered a book of physics. Many individual sciences, such as physics and psychology, once formed part of philosophy but are now separate academic disciplines. Toward the end of the modern period the term acquired its narrower meaning, associated mainly with metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics, and distinguished from the empirical sciences and mathematics.

Influential traditions include Western, Arabic–Persian, Indian, and Chinese philosophy. Western philosophy originated in ancient Greece. A central topic in Arabic–Persian philosophy is the relation between reason and revelation. Indian philosophy combines the spiritual problem of how to reach enlightenment with the exploration of the nature of reality and the ways of arriving at knowledge. Chinese philosophy focuses principally on practical issues about right social conduct, government, and self-cultivation.

The major branches are [[Epistemology]], which studies what knowledge is and how to acquire it; [[Ethics]], which investigates moral principles and right conduct; [[Logic]], the study of correct reasoning; and [[Metaphysics]], which examines the most general features of reality, existence, objects, and properties. Other subfields include aesthetics, philosophy of language, mind, mathematics, science, religion, and history, and political philosophy. Within each branch, competing schools promote different principles, theories, or methods. Philosophers use conceptual analysis, reliance on common sense and intuitions, thought experiments, analysis of ordinary language, description of experience, and critical questioning. Philosophy also informs fields such as law, business, and journalism by addressing their ethical questions.

Attempts to define philosophy precisely are controversial and are studied in metaphilosophy. Some definitions focus on method, such as pure reasoning, and others on topic. [[Immanuel Kant]] held that its task is united by four questions: "What can I know?", "What should I do?", "What may I hope?", and "What is the human being?" Naturalistic philosophers such as W. V. O. Quine see it as an empirical yet abstract science, and it has been described as "the midwife of the sciences." Others regard it as conceptual analysis, finding the necessary and sufficient conditions for applying concepts, or as thinking about thinking.

Ancient Semitic-speaking maritime civilization of city-states along the Levantine coast of the eastern Mediterranean, primarily in present-day Lebanon.

The Phoenicians emerged directly from the Bronze Age [[Canaan|Canaanites]], and their cultural traditions survived the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]]. They called themselves Canaanites and their land Canaan. *Phoenicia* is a Greek exonym, from *phoînix*, which meant variously "Phoenician person," "Tyrian purple, crimson," or "date palm"; it did not correspond to a unified native identity. Modern scholarship generally views the distinction after c. 1200 BC as artificial.

Phoenician society was organized into independent city-states, notably Byblos, Sidon, and Tyre, each politically autonomous, with no evidence of a shared national identity. The Phoenicians established one of antiquity's most extensive maritime networks, active for over a millennium and linking Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. They founded colonies and trading posts from Cyprus to the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula; [[Carthage]] became a major power by the 7th century BC. Exports included cedar wood, linen, and the dye [[Tyrian purple]].

The cities flourished most in the 9th century BC and subsequently declined under the expansion of empires such as the Neo-Assyrian and Achaemenid. [[Alexander the Great]] besieged Tyre in 332 BC. Phoenician influence nevertheless endured in the western Mediterranean until the Roman destruction of Carthage in the mid-2nd century BC.

Because little native literature survives, the Phoenicians were long regarded as a "lost" civilization and became better understood only after the discovery of inscriptions in the 17th and 18th centuries. Their most enduring legacy is the earliest verified alphabet, a 22-consonant script derived from the Proto-Sinaitic script. It spread across the Mediterranean and gave rise to the [[Greek alphabet]], ancestor of the Latin and Cyrillic scripts.

Art, application, and practice of creating images by recording light, either electronically by an image sensor or chemically on a light-sensitive material such as [[Photographic film]].

A lens focuses light reflected or emitted from objects into a real image on a light-sensitive surface inside a camera during a timed exposure. With an electronic sensor, this produces an electrical charge at each pixel. With photographic emulsion, it produces an invisible latent image that is chemically developed into a negative or positive; a negative is traditionally used to make a positive print on paper by enlarger or contact printing.

The word derives from Greek roots meaning "light" and "drawing." Its earliest known appearance in print was in a German newspaper article of February 25, 1839; the astronomer John Herschel is also credited with coining it that year.

The [[Camera obscura]] dates back to ancient China; Aristotle and Euclid described it in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. [[Ibn al-Haytham]] gave the first correct analysis of the phenomenon and invented the first true pinhole camera. In June 1802 Thomas Wedgwood made the first known attempt to capture a camera image with a light-sensitive substance. [[Nicéphore Niépce]] made the first known permanent photograph, *View from the Window at Le Gras*, around 1826 on a bitumen-coated pewter plate. In 1839 [[Louis Daguerre]] announced the daguerreotype while William Henry Fox Talbot independently developed the calotype negative-positive system, which allowed multiple prints.

[[George Eastman]] introduced roll film in 1888. Digital capture began with the [[Charge-coupled device]] in the 1960s, followed by consumer [[Digital photography]] in the 1990s. Digital manipulation and AI generation have raised debates over the authenticity of images.

Elementary particle that is a quantum of the electromagnetic field, including light and radio waves, and the force carrier of the electromagnetic force.

Photons are massless and can move at only one speed in a vacuum, the speed of light. The photon belongs to the class of [[Boson|bosons]]. Photons exhibit [[Wave–particle duality|wave–particle duality]], behaving as both waves and particles.

The modern concept originated in the first two decades of the 20th century with the work of [[Albert Einstein]], who built on the research of [[Max Planck]]. Planck proposed that the energy stored in a material object is composed of an integer number of discrete, equal-sized parts. To explain the photoelectric effect, Einstein introduced the idea that light itself is made of discrete units of energy. In 1926 [[Gilbert N. Lewis]] popularized the term *photon* for these units. The concept has led to advances including [[Laser|lasers]], Bose–Einstein condensation, quantum field theory, and quantum cryptography.

The photon has no electric charge, is generally considered to have zero rest mass, and is stable. The experimental upper limit on its mass is on the order of 10⁻⁵³ g, and its lifetime would be more than 10¹⁸ years. Photons obey Bose–Einstein statistics, so more than one can occupy the same quantum state.

Photon energy is proportional to frequency (*E* = *h*ν, where *h* is the Planck constant), and its energy and momentum are related by *E* = *pc*. A photon carries spin angular momentum of either +ħ or −ħ, corresponding to the two pure states of circular polarization; its independence from frequency was verified experimentally by [[C. V. Raman]] and Suri Bhagavantam in 1931. Collision of a particle with its antiparticle creates at least two photons.

Biological process by which photopigment-bearing organisms, such as most plants, algae, and [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]], convert light energy, typically from sunlight, into chemical energy.

The term usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, which releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. The converted energy is stored in the bonds of organic compounds, typically carbohydrates such as glucose, starches, and cellulose. It maintains the oxygen content of Earth's atmosphere and supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life.

The process begins when light energy is absorbed by reaction centers, proteins containing photosynthetic pigments. In plants these pigments are [[Chlorophyll|chlorophylls]], which absorb the red and blue spectra and so reflect green, held inside [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] in leaf cells. In the light-dependent reactions, energy is used to strip electrons from water, producing oxygen gas, and to create NADPH and ATP. In the light-independent reactions, called the Calvin cycle, atmospheric [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] is incorporated into existing organic compounds such as ribulose bisphosphate and reduced to carbohydrates.

Some organisms perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, which produces no oxygen. Purple bacteria split hydrogen sulfide, releasing sulfur instead. Archaea such as *Halobacterium* use retinal to absorb green light and power ATP synthesis; this form might have been the earliest to evolve.

The first photosynthetic organisms probably used hydrogen or hydrogen sulfide rather than water. Cyanobacteria appeared later, and the excess oxygen they produced contributed directly to the oxygenation of the Earth. Global photosynthesis captures energy at an average rate of approximately 130 terawatts, about eight times the total power consumption of human civilization. Jan Ingenhousz discovered photosynthesis in 1779, showing that plants need light, not just soil and water.

Branch of chemistry that studies macroscopic and microscopic phenomena in chemical systems in terms of the principles of physics, such as motion, energy, force, time, [[Thermodynamics]], [[Quantum chemistry]], [[Statistical mechanics]], and [[Chemical equilibrium|chemical equilibria]].

In contrast to chemical physics, it is predominantly, but not always, a supra-molecular science, since most of its founding principles concern bulk matter rather than molecular or atomic structure alone, as in [[Colloid|colloids]]. It studies, for example, how intermolecular forces affect plasticity, tensile strength, and surface tension.

A key concept is that chemical compounds can be described as groups of atoms bonded together and reactions as the making and breaking of those bonds. Predicting the properties of compounds from their atoms and bonds is a major goal. Quantum chemistry applies quantum mechanics to determine how strong and what shape bonds are, how nuclei move, and how light is absorbed or emitted by a compound. [[Spectroscopy]] is the related subdiscipline concerned with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter. Chemical thermodynamics sets limits on how far a reaction can proceed.

[[Chemical kinetics]] concerns which reactions occur and how fast. Most species must pass through transition states higher in energy than reactants or products; the higher the barrier, the slower the reaction. Statistical mechanics explains why a mixture of a very large number of particles (of the order of the Avogadro constant, 6 × 10²³) can often be described by a few variables such as pressure, temperature, and concentration.

The term was coined by [[Mikhail Lomonosov]] in 1752, when he presented a lecture course titled *A Course in True Physical Chemistry* to students at Petersburg University. Modern physical chemistry originated in the 1860s to 1880s.
